One-off property tax rebate for all owner-occupied residential properties in 2027
article:
The government has announced a one-off tax rebate for residential properties in 2027. HDB flats will get a 15% rebate, while private residences will receive a 10% rebate, capped at $100.

The rebate is aimed at cushioning property tax payments for Singaporeans amidst cost-of-living concerns, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) said in a Nov 23 release.

It added that as part of the government’s  yearly review, the annual values of HDB  flats have been updated to "better reflect prevailing market rents in their respective HDB towns”.

According to MOF, owner occupiers living in three-room and larger HDB flats will see an average property tax increase of about $2 to $4 per month, after the property tax rebate. One- and two-room HDB owner-occupiers do not pay property taxes.

Meanwhile, most owner-occupiers in private housing will see an average property tax increase of about $6 per month, MOF said.

The rebates will be automatically offset against owners’ 2027 property tax bill, which will be issued by December this year.

Separately, MOF also announced an increase in the annual value threshold used to assess eligibility for social support schemes.

Currently, various government social support schemes may use the annual value of the residential property as part of their criteria to provide tiered benefits to Singaporeans, with those living in properties with lower annual values receiving more support. These include the permanent GST Voucher scheme, MediShield Life premium subsidies, and the Workfare Income Supplement scheme.

With effect from Mar 1, 2027, the annual value threshold will be revised to $24,000 for the first tier ( up rom $21,000 currently) and to more than $24,000 and up to $32,000 for the second tier (from more than $21,000 and up to $31,000 currently).

" The increase will ensure that Singaporeans living in HDB flats and lower-value private properties will remain eligible for social support schemes, notwithstanding updates to the annual value of their homes," the ministry asaid.

title: Ang Mo Kio Library opens at AMK Hub with double-volume space and interactive exhibits
article:
Ang Mo Kio Library has opened at its new location on Level 4 of AMK Hub, occupying a space that previously housed a cinema.

The relocated library was officially opened on Nov 20 by Josephine Teo, Minister for Digital Development and Information.

It is the first public library in Singapore to feature a double-volume space throughout its main area, with floor-to-ceiling bookshelves lining the walls and more than 5,500 pre-loved books displayed on the upper shelves.

The library also offers more seating than its previous location along Ang Mo Kio Avenue 6 , including seven bookable study nooks, communal workspaces and individual study stations.

Design inspired by Ang Mo Kio's history

The interiors of the library draw inspiration from the neighbourhood's landmarks and green spaces, with design elements referencing its past.

Its curved entrance is inspired by Block 259 Ang Mo Kio Avenue 2 , better known as the Clover Block, the only circular block of flats built by HDB.

In the children's section, vehicle-shaped bookshelves, road markings and traffic signs recall the former Traffic Garden at Ang Mo Kio Town Centre in the 1980s.

Another key feature is the 6m-tall Immersive Hub, which has a curved exterior lined with pre-loved books. Inside, a 360-degree screen presents digital exhibits tracing Ang Mo Kio's development from a kampong settlement into a residential town.

Visitors can also explore archival photographs brought to life using AIartificial intelligence (AI), or create personalised videos imagining themselves in a future Ang Mo Kio.

Nearby, an 18m-long mural depicts familiar landmarks, including the former Broadway Cinema. Visitors can scan codes embedded in the artwork using the National Library & Archives Board (NLB) Mobile app to access recommended reading lists and borrow titles from the library's Singapore Collection.

“At the relocated Ang Mo Kio Library, we have drawn inspiration from the neighbourhood's familiar landmarks and rich heritage to create a space that truly represents Ang Mo Kio,” says Melissa Tam, chief executive officer of the NLB.

Extended opening hours

From Nov 21, the library is offering extended access beyond its regular operating hours of 11am to 9pm.

Visitors can enter designated areas from 9am using their NLB Mobile app or library card, while the Study Zone will remain accessible until 10pm daily, including public holidays.

The library's relocation is part of NLB's 15-year Libraries of the Future Masterplan to upgrade older libraries. Its new location at AMK Hub provides direct access to Ang Mo Kio MRT Sstation and the bus interchange.

title: 8 Things Analysts Are Telling Us About NAM CHEONG
article:
Nam Cheong’s shares (68 cents, -28% year-to-date) have been under pressure, even as more of its offshore support vessels return to work: fleet utilisation rose to
85% in 3Q2026
.
November 2026 reports from DBS and CGS International describe improving demand alongside stubborn costs and differing valuations.
The CGS report points out opportunities for Nam Cheong from renewed Malaysian oil drilling activity and the vessel-construction pipeline.
But it also gives weight to the reasons investors may remain cautious: higher costs, substantial construction funding needs, and lower sector valuation multiples.
Here are eight messages for investors:

85% in 3Q2026

S$1.45

2. The chartering recovery is visible

Fleet utilisation reached
85% in 3Q2026
, up from 70% a year earlier and 65% in 1H2026.
Chartering gross margin recovered to
51.5%, from 44.3%
in the first half, despite elevated Middle East operating costs.
Three vessel additions during the quarter lifted the fleet to 38, with 24 on long-term contracts.

3. Headline profit needs closer inspection

Reported quarterly attributable profit rose 31% to RM59.9 million, helped by RM21.9 million of insurance recovery.
DBS puts core profit at
RM48 million, down 15%
; CGS estimates
RM45.2 million, down 18%

4. Costs have prompted earnings cuts

Meghana KANDE
CGS lowers its 2026 core-profit forecast by

and its 2027 forecast by

Higher Middle East vessel costs and staff expenses are the reasons.
Significantly, it raises its 2027 revenue forecast while cutting profit expectations.

5. Malaysian drilling activity supports demand

CGS reports that Petronas and related companies awarded
14 rig contracts
during the year to date, compared with three in 2025.
Average Malaysian rig utilisation increased to 80%, from 73% in 2025.
More drilling should create work for support vessels.
CGS raises Nam Cheong’s 2027 fleet-utilisation assumption to 72%, from 70%.
CGS calls Nam Cheong “well-positioned for an earnings uplift from improving offshore contracting”.

title: Your CPF LIFE Payout Is Just the Beginning: 3 Ways to Build More Retirement Income
article:
Retirement
feels real, especially as you enter your 40s.
Even if you haven’t planned anything, the Singapore government provides a baseline retirement plan for most Singaporeans and permanent residents (PRs): Central Provident Fund (CPF) LIFE.
While it delivers lifelong monthly payouts, the amount is often insufficient for everyday expenses.
Hence, most retirees require complementary income streams.
Start by Understanding Your CPF LIFE Income Gap
How much your CPF LIFE pays depends on your CPF savings, payout plan, and payout start age.
Say you need S$3,500 a month in retirement, but CPF LIFE pays you only S$2,000 a month, leaving you with a shortfall of S$1,500 monthly, or S$18,000 annually.
This income gap matters.
This shortfall can widen over time as inflation, healthcare costs, and lifestyle needs push expenses up.
Knowing your shortfall helps determine how much additional savings or investment income you need.
Here are three ways you can bridge it:
#1: Build a Portfolio of Singapore Dividend Stocks
Blue-chip companies with long dividend histories – like
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05),
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), and
Singapore
Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68) – can provide regular
dividend income
.
To generate S$6,000 in annual dividends, you need:
S$200,000 at 3% dividend yield; or
S$150,000 at 4% dividend yield; or
S$120,000 at 5% dividend yield.
While higher yields require less capital, unusually high yields can signal financial trouble and future payout cuts.
Look beyond headline yields by assessing payout ratios, free cash flow, balance sheet strength and earnings resilience across economic cycles.
Dividends are not guaranteed, and companies can reduce or suspend payouts.
Avoid over-relying on one stock or sector for income by diversifying your investments.
#2: Use Singapore REITs to Generate Rental Income
Singapore real estate investment trusts
(S-REITs) let you earn rental income without buying physical property.
REITs that distribute at least 90% of their taxable income can enjoy tax transparency, so the REIT itself isn’t taxed on that income.
Some S-REITs that retirees can consider include:
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), which owns retail and office properties, and has a 5.1% yield
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U), which focuses on suburban retail properties, with a 5.9% yield
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU), which owns healthcare properties, with a 3.9% yield
A S$100,000 REIT portfolio that yields 5% generates S$5,000 in additional annual income, distributed quarterly or semi-annually.
Before investing in S-REITs, check occupancy rates and rental reversions and the sustainability of distribution per unit (DPU) to assess whether rental income is likely to remain resilient.
Pay attention to gearing levels, interest coverage and refinancing schedules.
Be wary of unusually high distribution yields caused by falling unit price, as this often reflects weaker property performance or financial difficulties.
#3: Build a Safer Income Layer with SSBs and T-Bills
Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs) and Singapore Treasury bills (T-bills) are government-backed, lower-risk alternatives to equities.
Both help retirees plan for shorter-term financial needs, preserve capital while earning interest, and provide stability to the portfolio during market downturns.
SSBs pay interest every six months and can be redeemed in any month, subject to the redemption process and fees.
T-bills, which are short-term government securities, lock in a fixed return when held to maturity.
However, both offer limited long-term income growth, and T-bill reinvestment rates drop when interest rates fall.
Putting It Together: A Retirement Income Portfolio
Excluding CPF LIFE, here is how S$400,000 in investable savings could be allocated:

Note: The 2.5% assumed for SSBs and T-bills is above current rates: the December 2026 SSB averages 2.39% a year over 10 years, while the 6-month T-bill cut-off yield was 1.86% on 4 November 2026.
This portfolio generates an annual income of S$14,750, or S$1,229 monthly.
Combined with the S$2,000 monthly CPF LIFE payouts, this brings total monthly income to S$3,229, leaving a shortfall of S$271 against the S$3,500 target.
A retiree could close this gap by trimming expenses or tapping additional savings.
As dividends are neither paid monthly nor guaranteed, retirees should keep payouts in a cash account to draw on when needed.
Retirees should also maintain a separate emergency cash reserve to avoid selling investments at bad times when they have unexpected cash needs.
Get Smart: Let CPF LIFE Be Your Foundation, Not Your Limit
CPF LIFE is a dependable starting point, not a complete retirement plan.
Combining Singapore dividend stocks, S-REITs, SSBs and T-bills allows retirees to diversify their cash flow while balancing yield against capital preservation and liquidity.
Ultimately, a comfortable retirement depends not just on how much CPF LIFE pays, but on how effectively you build and manage other income streams around it.

title: 3 Temasek-Backed Stocks Delivering Bigger Payouts This Week
article:
A rising dividend is pleasant, but one that can rise again is even more useful.
This week, three stocks with Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, among their shareholders will make payouts.
All three have raised their payouts over the past year, but the key question is what funded each increase and whether it can happen again.
As at 11 March 2026, Temasek held a 21.2% deemed interest in
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU) through Keppel Ltd and related companies.
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05), or DBS, counted Temasek as a 28.3% shareholder as at 10 February 2026, held directly and through Maju Holdings.
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68), or SGX, has a different ownership arrangement, with SEL Holdings holding 23.35% of SGX as at 1 September 2026.
Temasek has described SEL as a special purpose entity that it owns, holding the shares for the Financial Sector Development Fund without voting rights.

All three have already passed their record dates, so buying their shares or units now will not qualify you for this week’s payouts.
Can Keppel DC REIT keep growing its DPU?
As at 30 September 2026, Keppel DC REIT owned 27 data centres across 10 countries, including Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5.
On 23 November 2026, it will pay an advanced distribution of S$0.02261 per unit for the period from 1 July to 9 September 2026.
The REIT made this payment to ensure that income earned before its private placement went only to existing unitholders.
As the distribution covers just 71 days, there is no like-for-like comparison.
The full-period figures tell you more, with distribution per unit (DPU) for the first half of 2026 (1H2026)
rising 11.3%
year on year (YoY) to S$0.05714.
For the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), DPU climbed 11.7% to S$0.08571.
Most of that growth was earned, with rental reversions coming in at around 14% for 9M2026 and the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3 adding income.
For 9M2026, net property income (NPI) rose 13.1% YoY to S$316.8 million, ahead of DPU growth.
So where did the gap go?
Distributable income rose 16.7%, but DPU grew a slower 11.7%.
This is because the S$625 million placement enlarged the unit base before Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5 began contributing on 1 October 2026.
Management expects the acquisition to lift DPU by 2.0% on a pro forma basis.
Aggregate leverage would be 38.8% on a pro forma basis, including loans drawn on 1 October 2026, up from 36.2% as at 30 September 2026.
Is SGX’s dividend increase locked in?
SGX earns fees from listing, trading, clearing and settling shares in Singapore, as well as from derivatives and fixed income, currencies and commodities (FICC).
On 23 November 2026, it will pay S$0.1175 per share for the first quarter of its financial year ending 30 June 2027 (1QFY2027).
That is 9.3% more than the S$0.1075 paid for the same quarter a year earlier.
The increase was planned, as
SGX
has guided for a S$0.0025 rise in its dividend each quarter through FY2028.
On that schedule, its FY2027 dividend would add up to S$0.485.
That makes SGX’s increase the most predictable of the three, but it is still a plan rather than a guarantee, although SGX has said it is confident of delivering the increases through FY2028.
Keep FY2026’s one-off dividend of S$0.125 separate, as it came from capital recycling gains and lifted the full-year payout to S$0.57.
Investors should not budget for that extra payment to recur.
Falling interest rates are another risk, as SGX earns treasury income on collateral balances, which rose S$4.5 million in FY2026.
Can DBS keep lifting its ordinary dividend?
DBS serves retail, wealth and corporate customers across Asia.
On 24 November 2026, DBS will pay an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), up 10.0% from S$0.60 a year earlier.
It will also pay an unchanged capital return dividend of S$0.15, bringing the total to S$0.81, which is 8.0% higher than the S$0.75 paid a year earlier.
Here’s the thing:
the payout rose even as quarterly profit fell
.
Total income slipped 1.5% YoY to S$5,845 million, while net profit fell 4.8% to S$2,813 million.
Trading was responsible for most of the decline, with markets trading non-interest income dropping to S$17 million from S$419 million.
The core business continued to grow, with customer loans rising 9.5% to S$478.6 billion and net fee and commission income increasing 6% to S$1.43 billion.
For 9M2026, net profit rose 2% to a record S$8.82 billion.
For 2027, CFO Chng Sok Hui expects net interest income growth close to the mid-single digits, although DBS CEO Tan Su Shan cautioned that the outlook has become more uncertain.
With the capital return dividend unchanged, growth in the ordinary dividend is the figure to watch, as it will show whether profit is keeping pace.
Get Smart: Check what paid for the raise
A bigger payout is worth celebrating only once you know what funded it.
For a REIT, compare DPU growth with changes in the unit count, because a placement spreads income across more units.
For a bank, compare ordinary dividend growth with profit growth.
For SGX, remember that a pre-announced increase is still a plan, not a guarantee.
If rental reversions slow or trading volumes fade next year, which of these payouts would you still expect to rise?

title: Taiwan stocks see biggest leverage unwind in at least 30 years
article:
(Nov 23): Taiwan stocks saw the biggest unwind of leveraged bets in at least three decades on Friday, helping to explain why the authorities’ efforts to stem the selloff in Asia’s most tech-heavy market are having a limited impact.

The amount of outstanding margin loans — money that investors have borrowed from brokers to bet on equities — slumped by 49 billion Taiwan dollars (US$1.5 billion) on Friday, a record one-day decline based on data compiled by Bloomberg starting in 1996. The total has now tumbled more than 30% from a record high of around 653 billion Taiwan dollars set in October.

Taiwan’s benchmark stock index swung between gains and losses on Monday after sliding 17.5% last week, the biggest one-week decline since 1991. The island’s equity market has had a whipsaw year, first rallying on optimism over the artificial intelligence trade before being sold off due to concern over the heavy spending needed to fund the AI rollout.

“Retail leverage has fallen sharply, but margin-call and forced-deleveraging risks remain elevated,” Alvin So, a strategist at Goldman Sachs Group Inc in Hong Kong, wrote in a research note published Saturday. The market’s aggregate maintenance margin ratio has fallen to 132%, close to the 130% margin-call threshold, with 53% of stocks now below this level, he said.

title: Gold deluge keeps China’s US$1 tril trade surplus in check
article:
(Nov 23): China’s gold imports surged to a record US$209 billion ($269.6 billion) so far this year, in an unprecedented buying spree that followed a promise by top officials to make their country into the world’s marketplace instead of just its factory.

The shift began in January — the same month Vice-Premier He Lifeng made that vow in front of a crowd at Davos — as the value and volume of bullion imports more than doubled from the month before. Non-monetary gold purchases continued climbing in the 10 months through October, reaching a historical high that’s equivalent to nearly 8% of overall imports in the period, the latest data showed Friday.

As tensions with major trading partners like the European Union threatened to boil over, the deluge of gold has, in effect, helped keep China’s trade surplus from straying too far above last year’s record. Were it not for gold — which unlike other goods also serves as a financial asset or store of wealth — the difference between exports and imports would have crossed the US$1 trillion mark already in September instead of passing the milestone a month later.

“At a time when China’s record trade surplus has attracted growing scrutiny from its trading partners, higher gold imports mechanically reduce the headline merchandise trade surplus and its ratio to GDP,” said Tommy Xie, an economist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp Ltd. This could “provide some marginal relief” to disagreements over trade, he said.

Without the accumulation of gold, China would run a surplus of US$1.5 trillion for the full year, according to Brad Setser, a former US Treasury official now at the Council on Foreign Relations. At the current pace, however, the imbalance will likely come in at US$1.3 trillion, he estimates.

See also: China lowers margin requirement to 80% to boost stock liquidity

As the world’s top producer and consumer of gold, China strictly controls the flows of physical bullion, with the central bank issuing quotas to a select list of lenders. The exact volumes and other details of its allocations aren’t public.

“It was a really sharp run-up, so it does suggest some kind of policy shift, not organic change,” Setser said. “It is certainly plausible that quotas were expanded to allow more imports to reduce the trade surplus.”

The People’s Bank of China and the General Administration of Customs didn’t immediately reply to faxed requests for comment.

See also: China objects to US curbs on telecoms’ access to phone numbers

China’s overall trade surplus is still on course to exceed last year’s record of US$1.2 trillion, even as the value of imports surged 29% in the first 10 months of 2026 from a year ago, following a long stretch of stagnation or declines since 2022.

Besides the gold buying, soaring global prices of energy, metals and chips also inflated the improvement in purchases from abroad, masking persistent weakness in domestic demand. In volume terms, imports actually contracted in August and September. By contrast, while exports also received a boost from prices, their volumes have grown thanks to strong external demand.

Chinese households have flocked to gold in recent years during a prolonged slump in traditional stores of value like property. Demand has remained resilient this year even as bullion became less expensive, causing the local premium over global benchmarks to widen.

The precious metal has lost about a third of its value since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs stoked inflation and pushed expectations for rate cuts further into the future. It tumbled nearly 9% last week, after hitting its lowest level since September 2025.

In China, higher local prices and a stronger yuan made it cheaper for a select list of importers to buy gold overseas. A new licensing regime from June also gave banks more flexibility in using the quotas.

Jewellery now accounts for less than a third of China’s bullion demand, according to the World Gold Council. It’s total jewellery consumption in the first half was the weakest in two decades.

Instead, investment has become a major catalyst for China’s gold demand over the past two years, with bullion used less for consumption purposes. But that means China is “importing a financial asset in a way that registers in the goods data and reduces the reported surplus”, said Setser.

Hong Kong, Switzerland, Australia and South Africa have been the biggest exporters of gold into China, according to official data.

Apart from non-monetary gold, or bullion that’s held privately, the PBOC has also been buying the precious metal for two years straight. It was the biggest disclosed buyer among global central banks in the third quarter and its purchases in October were the largest in three years, though imports by monetary authorities are excluded from the goods trade balance.

With global attention trained on the imbalances generated by China, the gold build-up has helped create the appearance of rebalancing trade. Facing a protectionist backlash abroad, President Xi Jinping vowed at the APEC summit last week to cut tariffs, expand market access and foster a more stable environment for foreign investments.

“Gold imports are expected to remain elevated,” said Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “Gold is now one of the few assets that China can still buy in large volume and that can also preserve value.”

title: Gold rebounds as tech rout spurs shift to havens, Treasury rally
article:
(Nov 23): Gold rebounded from its biggest weekly decline in eight months as a technology-stock rout pushed traders to seek haven assets, driving down US Treasury yields and the dollar.

Bullion rose as much as 2.6% to around US$3,630 an ounce, after falling 9% last week to a 14-month low. Treasuries rallied on Friday, with traders seeking safety as growing concerns about artificial intelligence spending rippled across markets and sent technology stocks plunging.

Following the sell-off, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the Federal Reserve (Fed) risks jeopardising the US economy by overtightening in response to the latest inflation data. His prior attempt to rein in elevated long-term borrowing costs sent yields lower in August, which sparked a brief rally in gold.

Swaps traders have since pared their bets on a Fed rate hike in December as concerns grow that the financial market volatility may spill over to the broader economy. The policy-sensitive two-year yields ended 12 basis points lower on Friday, easing downward pressure on gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

The yellow metal has fallen by around a third since the US-Iran war erupted in late February as higher energy costs fuelled inflation, prompting central banks to raise rates. It’s traded below the US$4,000-an-ounce support level since Nov 11, as cratering tech stocks pushed traders to liquidate holdings to cover losses elsewhere. A gauge of the dollar had also risen almost 2% in November before easing on Monday, which had made bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers.

“If history is any guide, the past 13 weeks’ crash in gold is most likely exhausted for now,” said Adrian Ash, head of research at BullionVault, a platform for retail investors to buy gold. The company has seen strong dip-buying demand emerge from investors, he added.

See also: Gold set for worst week since March on hawkish Fed, AI sell-off

Spot gold rose 1.4% to US$3,587.13 an ounce at 10.14am in Singapore, while silver was up 1.9% at US$41.92 after tumbling 15% the week before. Platinum and palladium also advanced. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index dipped 0.1% after rising 0.6% last week.

title: ICICI Prudential seeks US$800 mil as alternatives push grows — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 23): ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co is seeking as much as US$800 million for private credit and special opportunities funds, according to people familiar with the matter, tapping growing demand for alternative assets from wealthy investors and institutions.

The Indian money manager aims to close its third private credit fund at about US$500 million in December and is separately seeking up to US$300 million for a special opportunities vehicle, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is private.

The potential fundraising underscores the growth of private credit in Asia, which has largely avoided turmoil elsewhere as funds tend to be closed-ended and have limited software exposure. Indian managers have raised billions of dollars and are taking a growing share of the country’s lending deals from global firms, intensifying competition for managers such as Bain Capital and Davidson Kempner Capital Management.

ICICI Prudential Corporate Credit Opportunities Fund has received commitments from more than a dozen insurance companies, as well as family offices and wealthy individuals, said the people. The fund focuses on performing credit rather than distressed situations, typically providing capital to borrowers for expansion and other capital expenditure, they said.

A spokesperson at ICICI Prudential AMC declined to comment. The firm is backed by ICICI Bank Ltd and Prudential Plc. The UK-listed insurer owns about a third of the Indian money manager through Prudential Corp.

ICICI Prudential AMC’s latest vehicle follows two private credit funds that raised about US$160 million and US$330 million, respectively, the people said. The manager has deployed money in companies including GMR Group, Puravankara Ltd and Pinnacle Industries Ltd, the people said. The companies did not respond to emails seeking comment.

See also: UK workers stay put as safety trumps pay in perilous jobs market

title: Oil edges lower as ample supply outweighs Middle East tensions
article:
(Nov 23): Oil dipped as traders weighed signs of robust crude exports against the prospect of escalating hostilities in the Middle East.

Brent traded around US$92 a barrel after closing 0.6% higher on Friday, while West Texas Intermediate was near US$83. There’s been a flare-up in low-level fighting recently, including frequent attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, although crude shipments are still flowing out of the Persian Gulf.

Global benchmark Brent has dropped by about a fifth this month after US President Donald Trump held off on renewed strikes following the US midterm elections. Still, he told a Fox News correspondent over the weekend that he’s inclined to resume attacks on Iran after the New Year if no deal is reached.

“Current flows out of the Middle East should see global oil inventories build,” said John Oh, an economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Still, “the market is currently pricing a US$25-to-US$30-a-barrel premium based on concerns that US-Iran fighting can escalate,” he added.

Over the weekend, Iran again attacked Bahrain, which hosts US forces, while Tehran-backed Houthi militants continued targeting Saudi Arabia, including the capital Riyadh. Trump said in a Truth Social post that the Islamic Republic fired more missiles and drones last week than at any time in more than a year.

Despite the hostilities, the supply outlook remains robust. The International Energy Agency has forecast a roughly two million-barrel-a-day surplus this quarter, while Goldman Sachs Group Inc has flagged the risk of a glut next year.

See also: Anthropic drops after IPO pop as AI slump engulfs markets
• Brent for January settlement was 0.3% lower at US$92.28 a barrel at 10am in Singapore.

- Futures fell 3.4% last week.

title: UK workers stay put as safety trumps pay in perilous jobs market
article:
(Nov 23): British workers are clinging to their jobs, accepting stagnant or falling pay in return for greater employment security amid the most challenging labour market in recent years.

Only two million people changed roles in the first nine months of 2026, according to official data. That’s below pre-pandemic levels and almost one million fewer than in the same period of 2022, when the reopening of the economy unleashed a surge of job-switching known as the Great Resignation.

They are choosing to stay put despite the possibility of earning thousands more elsewhere. A typical worker aged 35 or over has missed out on an extra £13,100 (US$17,200) a year by not changing employers more often, almost exactly the amount needed to feel financially comfortable, according to YouGov polling for hiring platform Employment Hero shared with Bloomberg. Almost a third said they’ve forgone £20,000 or more.

“Understandably, the cost of living is making people increasingly reluctant to take risks with their careers and this has come at a cost,” said Kevin Fitzgerald, UK managing director at Employment Hero.

Back in 2022, demand for labour gave workers bargaining power at a time of soaring inflation triggered by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, with even those who stayed in their roles often securing generous pay increases.

See also: South Korea’s early exports gain after US$1 tril milestone

For people now struggling with the Iran war cost-of-living crunch, things are very different. Vacancies are at their lowest in over five years, with AI and increased employment costs raising the bar to hiring workers, and wages are falling in real terms. The Bank of England (BOE) calls it a “low fire, low hire” labour market.

Just how much sway workers hold is a key question for the BOE as it tries to prevent the Middle East energy crisis from triggering an inflationary wage-price spiral. Rate-setters are keeping a close eye on wage negotiations early next year, when inflation is set to exceed 4%, but so far there is little evidence of second-round effects.

See also: Australian opposition calls for changes to gas reservation plan

Over 60% of British workers prioritise job security over ambitions to earn more, up from 58% last year, the Employment Hero survey found. While most received a wage rise in the past year, around half said it fell behind the cost of living, and only one in 10 said it outpaced it.

“Job-hugging” is not unique to the UK — in the US, rates of hiring, resignations and job-switching remain sluggish too. Economists fear the lack of mobility is making it harder for young people to get their first jobs or advance up the career ladder, with consequences for earnings and productivity.

“When fewer people move, labour market dynamism slows, the gains from having the right people in the right roles are left on the table, and businesses face less pressure to raise productivity to attract and keep staff,” said Nina Skero, chief executive of the Centre for Economics and Business Research think tank.

BOE deputy governor Clare Lombardelli recently noted that “people move less readily between jobs.” She said the long-running decline may mean workers are less well matched to vacancies.

Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG UK, said workers’ bargaining power “appears soft, with hiring intentions low and availability of staff high by historical standards.”

She added: “the recent transformation of the recruitment market has significantly lowered firms’ hiring costs while widening the pool of available candidates they can reach, adding to the downward pressure on future wage growth.”

title: South Korea’s early exports gain after US$1 tril milestone
article:
(Nov 23): South Korea’s exports extended gains in early November, with annual shipments topping US$1 trillion for the first time as the global artificial intelligence boom continued to stoke demand for chips.

Exports adjusted for working-day differences climbed 95.2% from a year earlier in the first 20 days of November, according to data released Monday by the customs office. That compared with an 65.9% increase during the same period in October.

On an unadjusted basis, outbound shipments climbed 101.5%, while imports rose 39.4%, resulting in a trade surplus of US$27.1 billion. Exports totalled US$77.4 billion in the first 20 days of this month, extending momentum after shipments reached US$61.7 billion during the same period in October.

The figures add to signs of resilience in South Korea’s trade-reliant economy, which has expanded faster than expected this year as surging AI infrastructure investment fuels demand for the country’s semiconductors. South Korea last week became the fourth country to surpass US$1 trillion in annual exports, after the US, Germany and China, the trade ministry said.

The latest trade data come just days before the Bank of Korea’s (BOK) final monetary policy meeting of the year on Nov 26, when economists expect policymakers to raise the policy rate by a quarter percentage point to 3.25%. The central bank held rates steady in October after consecutive increases in July and August, seeking to assess the impact of higher borrowing costs.

The strength of semiconductor demand has also prompted a wave of upgrades to South Korea’s economic outlook. State-run think tank Korea Development Institute last week sharply raised its growth forecast for 2027 to 3.9% from 2.2%, while the International Monetary Fund projected a 3.3% expansion next year.

See also: Australian opposition calls for changes to gas reservation plan

In Monday’s data, semiconductors remained the main engine of growth, with chip exports surging 294.4% from a year earlier to US$38.5 billion. Shipments of petroleum products increased 91.9%, while automobile exports dropped 5.6%.

The BOK is expected to revise its own growth and inflation forecasts at Thursday’s meeting, alongside an updated six-month interest-rate projection. In August, the central bank projected growth of 3.3% this year and 2.9% in 2027, but has since indicated that the economy is likely to expand considerably faster than previously expected.

South Korea’s economy grew 1% in the third quarter from the previous three months, beating economists’ expectations, as exports and investment surged. Still, private consumption contracted unexpectedly, underscoring how the benefits of the chip boom have yet to spread broadly to households.

See also: South Korea to ground flights, delay trading for college exam

Persistent inflation is adding to the case for further tightening. Consumer prices rose 2.8% in October from a year earlier, while core inflation held at 2.8%, leaving both measures above the BOK’s 2% target.

By destination, exports to China increased 145.6%, while shipments to the US rose 142.7%. Exports to Taiwan and Vietnam gained 149.7% and 85.8%, respectively.

title: US probing alleged spy tied to ex-Nvidia CEO, spy chief says
article:
(Nov 22): Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Nvidia Corp is a perpetual target for people trying to illegally obtain its high-end chips and the US is investigating an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with the company’s former chief executive.

“Nvidia chips, they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants,” Clayton said Sunday on ABC’s This Week. “That’s why we’re focusing on this. People will do a lot, they will break the law. There are indictments already involving other companies where people have broken the law to get access to Nvidia chips.”

He said in a separate interview on CNN’s State of the Union that Attorney General Todd Blanche has made it clear that the US is looking into Alice Huang, a former executive for Singapore-based Megaspeed International, and her company but declined to comment further.

“This is how we operate in America — to let that investigation play out,” he said on CNN. “And there is not only the DOJ investigation, but I’m sure the board of directors and Nvidia is looking into what happened. Regulatory agencies, let’s let all that play out. Let’s gather the facts.”

Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang was ousted from his job after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, while denying any wrongdoing.

Scott Bessent, on CBS’ Face The Nation, said he presumed the ousted CEO wasn’t aware of the spy allegations against Alice Huang and that the US has taken steps to close the policy loopholes that allowed high-end AI chips to get to Chinese entities. He also said Nvidia needs to conduct a robust internal investigation on how such sales were allowed to go on.

See also: Tower Records becomes latest Japan retailer hit by data breach

“It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was. Was there promiscuous attitude towards this, and where if it happened, where were the faults,” he told CBS on Sunday.

“Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers,” Bessent said.

See also: China’s US$1.7 tril AI rout turns hot trade into losing bet

More broadly, Clayton said the US needs to maintain its leadership when it comes to high-end chips, which means balancing export restrictions on the most sensitive technology while driving the buildout in artificial-intelligence technology internationally.

“We want to lead the globe in the build out of this infrastructure, but we also want to keep the most exquisite capabilities for America,” he said on ABC.

Jensen Huang is set to face questions from lawmakers over the company’s ties to China when he appears Dec 1 before a joint meeting of the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China Select committees. The session is expected to take place behind closed doors.

Republican Representative Michael McCaul said he aims to press Huang on whether Nvidia knew its advanced chips could end up in China in violation of US export controls.

“Did he know that these advanced chips that he was selling to Mega Speed were being sent into China in violation of export control laws?” McCaul said in an interview with Bloomberg This Weekend on Sunday.

McCaul added the broader concern is that access to cutting-edge US technology could help China reduce its reliance on American companies. “The problem is when you sell them our advanced technology, they can replicate that, they can reverse engineer it, and then they don’t need us,” he said.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under strong criticism, including from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, for lax enforcement of US export curbs on high-end chips. Clayton declined to comment on the Commerce Department’s record, saying he wouldn’t be drawn into internal administration deliberations.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

But Senator John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, said he wants to hear from Lutnick and Bessent about how Commerce was approaching export controls.

“It appears to me — emphasize, “appears” — that the Department of Commerce has allowed the Communist Party of China to circumvent our export controls on advanced chips, either that or they didn’t know what they were doing,” Kennedy said on NBC’s Meet the Press.

“Now, I don’t think they’re incompetent. It appears that they knowingly allowed this to happen. Scott Bessent has been saying, “Stop,” he added. “So I want to get both of them in front of a committee, put them under oath, ask them not to stab each other because I realize they don’t like each other, and let’s answer some hard questions. And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion.”

Separately, California is doing its own investigation into whether potential criminal violations of state law and whether Nvidia Corp. illegally sold advanced chips to China and misled investors about the conduct, its attorney general, Rob Bonta, told Bloomberg News in an interview.

title: Stoneweg European Stapled Trust acquires Verona Freight Village in Italy for EUR61 mil, 7% discount to valuation
article:
Stoneweg European Stapled Trust (SERT) has acquired a logistic facility in Verona, Italy, named Verona Freight Village, for a total consideration of EUR61 million ($86 million). The consideration carries a 7% discount to the independent valuation of EUR65.7 million as of Sept 22.

According to the manager, Verona Freight Village is a newly completed freehold logistics facility, with approximately 43,500 sqm of lettable area. The asset is fully leased to Stora Enso, which is a leading global provider of renewable solutions in packaging, biomaterials and sustainable construction.

It has a 15-year lease, with a mutual break option after year nine and annual rental indexation linked to 100% of Italian’s consumer price index (CPI). The lease has a net initial yield of approximately 6.0%, which is above current prime Italian logistics yields of 5.3% to 5.5%.

Following the acquisition, SERT’s exposure to logistics, light industrial and data-centre assets will increase from 62.8% to 63.8%, while Western Europe and the Nordics will account for 90.8% of the portfolio.

The manager says that the acquisition will be funded initially by its revolving credit facility. Moving ahead, it intends to refinance the acquistion financing through a combination of capital recycling initiatives, recovery of Italian value-added tax (VAT) within one year and other financial sources. Italy's VAT stands at 22%.

On a pro forma basis, assuming the acquisition was done on Jan 1, 2025 and fully funded by debt that carries an interest rate of 4.5%, SERT’s distribution per stapled security (DPS) will see an accretion of 0.68% if the Italian VAT is being reimbursed within 9 months.

See also: US office ‘still in recovery’ but Manulife US REIT aiming for next sale within six to eight months

Assuming the Italian VAT is fully recovered upon completion of acquisition, the DPS accretion will be higher at 1.22%.

“The transaction demonstrates our ability to redeploy capital into high-conviction opportunities that are immediately earnings accretive while advancing our target of achieving close to 80% exposure to the logistics, light industrial and data centre sectors by 2028,” says Simon Garing, CEO of the manager.

Units in SERT closed 4 Euro cents lower, or down 2.68% at €1.45 back on Nov 23.

title: Asia’s stock rescue efforts gather pace after Wall Street plunge
article:
(Nov 23) : Asian authorities are stepping up efforts to stem a deepening stock-market rout, with China easing margin requirements, and Taiwan and South Korea rolling out intervention measures following Friday’s plunge in US equities.

In China, the minimum margin requirement for investors buying securities with borrowed funds will fall to 80% from 100% on Nov. 30, according to notices issued on Sunday by the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges with approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission. The exchanges had raised the ratio to 100% from 80% in January to curb leverage risks.

Regulators said the latest adjustment is related to a marked decline in margin-financing activity and relatively low overall leverage. Brokerages can apply the revised rules to outstanding financing contracts when calculating available margin balances, while investors engaged in abnormal trading may face stricter requirements and other risk controls.

The change could unleash nearly 400 billion yuan (US$60 billion) in additional funds, the Xinhua News Agency reported Sunday, citing the regulator.

The moves add to a series of efforts by Beijing to restore confidence after a months-long rout pushed the benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market. The gauge tumbled over 8% in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade, as weakness in the economy and a sharp reversal in tech shares weighed on sentiment.

Also on Sunday, South Korea announced phased measures to calm markets amid rising volatility. The moves include ensuring a stock stabilization fund is in place to respond when needed, top financial officials said after an emergency meeting.

See also: Dip buyers hesitate to step in as Nasdaq 100 nears a bear market

Memory chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc. both fell over 5% in pre-market trading in Korea. Japanese markets are closed Monday for a holiday.

“The government is preparing preparing a 10 trillion won market stabilization fund, though the size looks insufficient to materially change near term sentiment,” said Shawn Oh, head of Korea cash equities at NH Investment & Securities. “A sustained return to tech likely requires clearer resolution of Nvidia-related uncertainty, evidence that AI demand remains resilient despite tighter US chip export to China, and geopolitical easing that brings oil meaningfully lower.”

Earlier, Taiwan widened curbs on short sales of local stocks and said it has been buying shares, stepping up efforts to revive confidence after the island’s benchmark index had its worst weekly fall in 35 years.

See also: Asia braces for more volatility after US selloff

China’s securities watchdog said this month that margin balances and trading activity had declined significantly and overall leverage had become more stable, creating room to optimize risk-control parameters under its countercyclical framework.

Meanwhile, the Shenzhen Stock Exchange is proposing introducing market makers on the ChiNext board, according to draft rules released for public comment. The system is intended to broaden the pool of market participants, improve liquidity and pricing efficiency, and strengthen the market.

China Securities Depository and Clearing Corp. will also continue to waive issuer service and settlement fees for green corporate bonds, tech corporate notes and private-enterprise corporate bonds, excluding convertible bonds, from the start of 2027 through the end of 2028.

The measures target different parts of the market. Lower margin requirements increase investors’ purchasing capacity, market maker moves are intended to bolster liquidity and reduce price volatility, while fee cuts lower transaction and financing-related costs. The efforts signal that authorities are broadening their toolkits as they seek to stabilize trading and investor expectations following the sharp decline.

The People’s Bank of China said this month it would conduct more than 100 billion yuan of swap operations to provide liquidity to securities firms, fund managers and insurers, while a relending program for share buybacks and stake increases was made a longer-term mechanism and its interest rate was cut to 1% from 1.25%.

Those measures have so far struggled to produce a sustained turnaround. The weakness reflects more than a shortage of market liquidity, with concerns about sluggish domestic demand, the prolonged property downturn and fading enthusiasm for the AI trade continuing to weigh on investor confidence.

Beijing’s latest moves suggest policymakers are sticking with a familiar playbook of targeted market support rather than a sweeping stimulus package. This time, however, the measures span leveraged buying, trading liquidity and transaction costs, broadening an effort to put a floor under the selloff and restore confidence in the world’s second-largest stock market.

title: Dip buyers hesitate to step in as Nasdaq 100 nears a bear market
article:
(Nov 23) : Since the fundamental outlook did not change dramatically during last week’s massive selloff in stocks and many valuation measures are now screaming bargain, contrarian impulses to buy the dip are running strong.

Yet for a lot of professional money managers, there are too many lingering questions heading into a holiday-shortened week of trading in the US to lend confidence to the idea that the bottom has been set after the Nasdaq 100 Index extended its drop from an Oct. 6 record to 19.8% and the S&P 500’s drawdown reached 12%.

Among those questions: Will the headlines continue to move beyond Jensen Huang’s personal life and into the financial decision made at Nvidia Inc. under his leadership? Will either sophisticated hedge funds or retail traders be willing to buy the dip Monday morning? Will the Federal Reserve follow through on raising interest rates as foreshadowed in speeches by several of its policymakers last week?

“The market is working through a stack of problems at once — inflationary pressures, a December rate hike, and renewed doubt about what AI returns actually look like in 2028 and 2029,” said Dave Mazza, chief executive officer at Roundhill Investments. “None of that resolves next week, and with no positive catalyst on the calendar, buyers have little reason to show up with conviction.”

At Goldman Sachs Group Inc., the equity trading desk is telling clients that panic like last week’s is usually a good opportunity to buy — but there are important differences with this setup. The first is that the Fed is in a hiking cycle. And secondly, investor positioning is complicated: While hedge funds are “overwhelmingly downbeat” and have cut leverage to a five-year low, other groups remain relatively well-invested and believe hedge funds will be forced to buy back in. So the Goldman traders suggest profiting from what may have been the worst of the volatility by selling put options rather than bottom-fishing in equities.

The selloff has also spread across systematic investors, with commodity trading advisers, or CTAs, selling an estimated US$57 billion in equities over the past month, according to Goldman’s estimates. Their net positioning in US stocks has turned short by US$19 billion. While systematic flows remain a source of selling pressure globally, most of the remaining risk is now concentrated outside the US. In the US, much of the selling has already taken place, and CTAs could become buyers if stocks rebound, Goldman’s models show.

See also: Asia braces for more volatility after US selloff

“We can make a pretty compelling argument that vol has overshot without necessarily having to call the bottom in equities,” the traders wrote in a note to clients.

That type of sentiment was echoed by many on the buy side.

“It feels like we are getting to the point that the selling may be exhausted and a bounce should be in the offing — but there are no real identifiable catalysts,” said Joe Gilbert, portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management. “A flat week next week may be a victory for the bulls.”

See also: Stocks fall as Anthropic debut not an AI all-clear

For many deciding whether to buy the dip, however, the first step is wrapping their heads around what created all that turbulence that crashed stocks and sent the Cboe Volatility Index to a 19-month high of almost 36 by the end of the week.

After all, there were high hopes that two events – Nvidia’s earnings report on Tuesday and Anthropic PBC’s stock market debut on Thursday – would revive confidence in the wobbling AI trade that had fueled the bull market for four years. Instead, the S&P 500 extended its losing streak to seven straight days, posting a weekly loss of 8.6% — its worst in 19 months.

For some, Anthropic’s record US$119.5 billion equity offering was too much for the market to handle, especially given the turmoil in the AI trade amid growing scrutiny of Huang and Nvidia.

“Anthropic sucked a massive amount of liquidity in an already weak AI narrative,” Daniel Kim, chief investment officer at Penserra Global Investors, said on Friday. “I read this week as a washout, and I think Anthropic was likely the final shoe to drop. Good news was sold all week, and by Friday hedges like gold were being sold alongside semis, which is the mark of forced selling. And that tends to exhaust itself quickly.”

Yet a short trading week upcoming in the US – markets are closed on Thursday and half of Friday for Thanksgiving – could also strain liquidity.

“I would not be surprised if the unwind continues through the shortened week, since thin holiday liquidity is a poor setting for the market to form a new view,” Kim added. “Once that selling has cleared, we could get a strong rally heading into Christmas.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Of course, much of the market’s sentiment will hinge on what more shoes may drop in the saga involving Jensen Huang and Nvidia. The chipmaker’s strong earnings report — total sales rose 103% in the latest quarter and revenue is expected to grow 75% in the next fiscal year – only led to a brief rebound in the shares before scrutiny of the company and its former leader continued to build throughout the week.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said on Thursday that the chipmaker is being investigated in his state to determine whether any of its actions resulted in advanced chips or confidential information being improperly obtained by China. His office is also looking into whether the company misled investors about the situation.

That same day, two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee asked the Commerce Department to turn over information regarding allegations that Nvidia tried to influence an inquiry into Megaspeed International, the cloud computing company linked to the woman who had a relationship with Huang.

And on Friday, Reuters reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission was probing the company over potential accounting issues.

Nvidia ended the week down 23%, its worst since 2008, and has lost 48% since Oct. 6.

Given the company’s crucial role as not only the seller of the most important chips used in AI, but also its significance as the “Bank of Nvidia” providing financing to a wide array of players in the industry, each negative headline hurt the broader market as well.

Traders watched as crucial technical levels like the 200-day moving average and even the round number of 7,000 offered no support to the S&P 500, which closed the week at a seven-month low of 6,910.39.

“I thought 7,000 had at least a real chance of being a level where the market would find support,” said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers. “Then the latest Nvidia stuff came out and it was ‘boom,’ like a knife through butter.”

To Keith Lerner, chief investment officer of Truist Advisory Services, it’s not that investors lost confidence in the long-term potential of AI last week, it’s that they lost confidence in the earnings forecasts that have been supporting stocks tied to the industry. And that loss of confidence is being amplified by a Fed that is signaling additional rate hikes.

Indeed, even as Nvidia and Anthropic captured most of the market’s attention during the week, many investors made note of a series of speeches by Fed policymakers with hawkish tones. On Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller even urged his colleagues to consider a larger, half-percentage-point rate hike at its December meeting.

“Perhaps the market is waking up to the idea that we’re actually in a rate hiking cycle,” said Roundhill’s Mazza.

Still, as investors prepare for a new week of trading, the question on many of their minds is when — not if — to buy the dip.

“We may see a bit more technical declines come on Monday or retail waking up and de-risking,” said Nadine Terman, chief executive officer of Solstein Capital, who expects declines to follow through in Asia and Europe at the start of the new week.

Yet she added: “I am just on the phone now with a client talking about timing for bottom feeding.”

title: From understanding futures to exploring them: Inside KGI Crusoe
article:
While retail investors here in Singapore are knowledgeable about the functions of an equity trading platform, however, they are still somewhat unfamiliar with how a futures trading platform works given that it is being considered as complex financial instruments that require specialised knowledge.

An equity trading platform typically provides investors the ownership to buy, hold and review while a futures trading platform focuses on managing risk, because every position is leveraged, marked to market daily, carries an expiry, and can be long or short.

This means that the interface has to answer different questions in real time, such as, what is each tick worth on this position, when does it expire and what happens if the price moves against the investor.

As such, tools such as depth-of-market price ladders, and bracket orders that attach a stop loss and profit target at entry, are standard on futures trading platforms and rare on equity trading platforms.

What to look out for in a futures trading platform

With that, the most important question to ask is this: “What should an investor look out for in a futures trading platform?”

One key aspect is to ensure that it should be operated by a locally licensed firm, and should be trading genuine exchange-traded, centrally cleared futures rather than an over-the-counter product such as a contract for differences (CFD).

Another factor would be the variety of asset classes that the platform can offer. In 1Q2026, CME Group recorded record volume in all six of its asset classes at the same time: interest rates, equities, energy, agriculture, metals and foreign exchange.

The final element to keep in mind is transparent all-in costs, including commissions, exchange fees and market data; a simulation environment on the same platform you will trade on; and education and support available in your own time zone.

With the recent new management direction, KGI Securities is launching its latest futures trading platform called KGI Crusoe.

“The technology behind KGI Crusoe is the key thing that makes its a KGI platform,” says Ken Ong, CEO of KGI Securities (Singapore). “Clients open their accounts with KGI, are onboarded and supported by our team in Singapore, and trade with a MAS-regulated broker,” he adds.

Ong shares that the product range, education, pricing plans and client protections are all designed by KGI Securities for Singapore investors. “To put it simply, the technology is world-class, and the experience is built for Singapore,” he describes.

Rather than convenience, the technology behind it plays a role in the overall risk management. “Leverage magnifies the cost of a delayed order or an unclear screen, and therefore, speed, reliability and clarity matter more than they do in equities,” he explains.

Ong adds that the reason for the technology to stand out is because it was built for futures from the ground up, and those capabilities now power KGI Crusoe.

“Traders get professional charting and analysis, a depth-of-market trading interface that shows where buyers and sellers are positioned at each price, and trade management features that can automatically attach stop-loss and profit-target orders to every position,” he elaborates.

Besides that, the display of margin requirements and contract specifications at every stage will allow traders to know what a position requires. Meanwhile, the same platform also offers simulated trading in live market conditions, so investors can learn and test strategies with no capital at risk before moving to a live account.

KGI Crusoe is available on the web, so traders can access the platform from any browser, including during the US session in the Singapore evening. Desktop and mobile apps will follow at the platform's full launch.

Following numerous conversations with Singapore investors, Ong sees three needs being stood out within the space.

“First, consolidation. Many futures traders rely on a patchwork of tools: charts in one application, execution in another, and education gathered from scattered sources online. KGI Crusoe brings learning, practice, analysis and trading onto a single platform,” Ong shares.

“Second, guidance. Futures have a reputation for a steep learning curve, and the data supports what we heard. A 2025 survey by the Securities Investors Association (Singapore) and Beansprout found that key barriers for beginner investors include a lack of familiarity and a lack of expert guidance. Practising in a simulated environment before committing capital, and understanding concepts like margin, contract size and expiry in plain terms, can go a long way in helping newer traders build confidence,” he adds.

“Lastly, a regulated, local home. With KGI Crusoe, investors can trade major CME Group markets through a MAS-regulated broker, with client support available during Singapore hours. Positions in physically deliverable contracts are also closed out ahead of delivery,” Ong mentions.

Based on his observations, Singapore is well positioned to become a regional centre for retail futures trading, supported by favourable time zones, credible regulatory framework and a financially sophisticated investor base.

“The regional demand is highly visible with CME Group's Asia-Pacific volume reaching a record 1.9 million contracts a day in 2025, then rising to an all-time high of 2.6 million in the first quarter of 2026,” Ong explains.

From his perspective, KGI Securities’ ambition is to make KGI Crusoe to become Singapore’s go-to home for futures trading. Ong believes that will require more than adding a product to the shelf. In fact, it will require a platform that provides education and service designed specifically around futures.

Ong sees the technology powering KGI Crusoe offers that complete experience from day one, while KGI Securities focuses on serving clients locally, operating to MAS standards and building the educational foundation investors need.

“Over time, we will continue to broaden the offering in response to what our clients need, with futures remaining at the center rather than on the side,” Ong shares.

KGI Crusoe: what it means for Singapore investors

KGI Crusoe's upcoming launch will make it easier for investors to access futures markets through a MAS-regulated Singapore broker, offering an alternative to overseas accounts and CFDs, according to Ong.

“Singapore investors now have a dedicated, locally regulated home for exchange-traded, centrally cleared futures on the world's leading derivatives exchanges,” he adds.

Ong sees a broader shift underway as the line between retail and institutional tools is disappearing.

Micro equity index contracts accounted for 40.5% of CME Group's equity index volume in December 2025, and new retail traders continue to enter the market.

“Our responsibility is to make sure that as access widens, understanding and protection widen with it. That is what KGI Crusoe stands for: giving every trader the tools, structure and confidence to build their own approach to the markets, and to do so responsibly,” Ong concludes.

title: Managing global equity exposure during Asian trading hours
article:
Global investing has long been shaped by geography. Capital flows across borders, but trading hours, market structures and liquidity remain largely anchored to individual financial centres. As institutional portfolios become more international, that distinction is becoming harder to ignore.

Consider an Asia-based investor with exposure to Japanese equities, U.S. companies and emerging markets. The underlying investments may span several continents, but risk mitigation and asset allocation often need to be implemented within the same trading day.

Managing those exposures efficiently is not simply a question of market access. It also depends on the availability of instruments that facilitate the management of global exposures during same trading hours. This is changing the role of Asia's derivatives markets. Singapore, already an established centre for trading Asian equity derivatives, is extending its reach into a broader range of global and regional exposures. The latest expansion of the three-decade partnership between MSCI and SGX Group (Singapore Exchange), which could bring up to 100 new futures and options contracts to the market, is one indication of that shift.

The expansion, announced in July 2026, initially comprised approximately 40 futures and options contracts covering global developed- and emerging-market benchmarks, key Asia-Pacific country size indexes, World and emerging-Asia sectors.

The introduction of these contracts marks a shift in how market participants manage international portfolios. By bringing a broad suite of global and regional benchmarks onto a single trusted platform, SGX is strengthening Singapore’s position as a global hub for derivatives trading and risk management.

“Today’s defining risk-management challenge is the compression of decision time,” says Janice Kan, Head of Derivatives at SGX Group. “Macroeconomic events can trigger continuous repricing across borders, and investors increasingly need to manage their exposures holistically before Western markets open. Just as global FX relies on London, New York and Singapore to support round-the-clock liquidity, global derivatives markets are evolving in the same direction. By building deep liquidity in global benchmarks during Asian trading hours, we enable institutional investors to respond as market conditions change.”

The index underlying a derivatives contract determines the exposure investors are taking. Even indexes tracking the same market can differ considerably in composition, coverage and liquidity — distinctions that matter when adjusting allocations or hedging portfolios.

Japan illustrates the point. After years of relative underperformance, Japanese equities have experienced a reversal amid monetary policy normalization and corporate governance reforms. According to MSCI research, the MSCI Japan Index outperformed the MSCI Kokusai (World ex Japan) Index by 15.7% from its January 2025 low through October 2026.

Yet the case for Japan extends beyond headline returns. Industrials account for approximately 25% of the MSCI Japan Index, more than twice their weight in the MSCI Kokusai Index. Japan also offers differentiated exposure to financials, semiconductor equipment, robotics and precision components.

Even within Japan, the choice of index can influence the investment outcome. The MSCI Japan Index covers large- and mid-cap companies, while the MSCI Japan Investable Market Index (IMI) extends into small caps. The MSCI Japan Select 700 Index occupies a middle ground, offering broader coverage than MSCI Japan while maintaining comparable underlying-basket liquidity under MSCI's analysis.

“Indexes covering the same market can represent it differently, resulting in distinct exposures and risk characteristics. Benchmark choice matters when investors use an index to shape allocations or manage portfolio risk,” said Priscilla Luk, Head of APAC Index at MSCI.

"Index design balances market representation with implementation criteria such as investability and liquidity. There is no single approach that suits every investment strategy. The right choice depends on the investor’s objectives and the exposure they want to capture.”

The growing use of equity derivatives also reflects a distinction between deciding where to invest and determining how to implement that decision.

An investor seeking to reduce exposure to a particular market, for example, may use index futures to hedge part of an existing portfolio rather than sell the underlying securities. Similarly, index derivatives can be used to adjust regional allocations or manage short-term risks around market events.

However, execution involves practical considerations. The liquidity of a contract, the characteristics of its underlying index and the costs of establishing or unwinding positions can all influence its suitability for a particular strategy.

For global institutions, execution efficiency is closely tied to the underlying infrastructure supporting it. Managing multiple regional exposures across fragmented trading venues creates operational friction and splits collateral. Bringing these MSCI-linked contracts under SGX’s clearing house allows participants to consolidate their positions within a single, regulated environment.

“Investors experience risk at the total portfolio level, not the product level,” says Kan. “When multiple asset classes and regional contracts are traded and cleared through a common infrastructure, institutions can consolidate positions and collateral more effectively. Our objective is to reduce the friction between investment intent and execution, enabling institutions to deploy, protect and reposition capital with greater efficiency and certainty.”

The next phase of global portfolio management

The evolution of equity derivatives markets reflects a broader shift in institutional investing. As portfolios become more global, investors increasingly need to consider not only which markets they want to access, but also how those exposures can be measured, traded and managed.

“For investors managing global portfolios from Asia, the challenge is to understand how equity exposures across markets combine and manage those exposures as markets move,” said Luk. “MSCI indexes provide a consistent framework for comparing exposures, while listed derivatives can help investors hedge or adjust positions during Asian trading hours.”

The expanded MSCI-SGX partnership brings together two essential elements of this process: indexes constructed under a consistent methodology to represent the global equity opportunity set, with an emphasis on investability and replicability, and derivatives infrastructure that enables investors to act on those exposures.

Global portfolios no longer fit neatly within regional trading hours. Increasingly, neither can the markets that support them. The next phase of derivatives market development will be shaped not just by what investors can trade, but by when, where and how efficiently they can manage their allocations.

title: Asia braces for more volatility after US selloff
article:
(Nov 23) :Traders in Asia were bracing for another bout of volatility after a sharp Wall Street selloff rattled risk appetite, even as regional authorities stepped up efforts to shore up markets.

The risk-sensitive Australian dollar edged lower in early trading while the Japanese yen was little changed. Equity-index futures pointed to pressure on Asian stocks after the S&P 500 entered a technical correction and the Nasdaq 100 posted its worst week since March 2020. The VIX Index, Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, surged to its highest since April 2025. Japanese markets are closed Monday for a holiday.

The retreat has fueled concern that the US technology selloff is broadening into a wider risk-off move, leaving Asian markets vulnerable. MSCI’s regional gauge is nearing a bear market after falling about 18% from its June peak, putting the focus on whether authorities can help restore confidence and stem further selling.

“This has been more than an ordinary pullback,” Greg Boland, a strategist at FUTU Holdings-owned Moomoo Securities, wrote in a note. “The speed and breadth of the selling suggest elements of capitulation, with investors increasingly focused on protecting capital rather than buying the dip. Whether this represents a selling climax or the beginning of a deeper market reset remains the critical question.”

Authorities across Asia stepped up efforts over the weekend to stem the deepening stock-market rout. China will ease minimum margin requirements for investors buying securities with borrowed funds, while Taiwan widened curbs on short selling and said it has been buying shares after the island’s benchmark suffered its worst weekly drop in 35 years.

South Korean authorities said they will ease daily limits on company share buybacks for three months and begin preparations to activate a stock-market stabilization fund if needed. The rescue fund was last used during the global financial crisis in 2008, according to local media.

See also: Stocks fall as Anthropic debut not an AI all-clear

The turmoil has rippled across global markets, engulfing metals and emerging-market assets while driving investors into havens including Treasuries. Risk-sensitive currencies have also been hit, with the Australian dollar erasing its gain for the year and the New Zealand dollar falling to its weakest since the GFC.

Investors are also looking ahead to US inflation data this week. Economists expect the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, to have risen 3.8% in October from a year earlier, according to the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. The figures are due Wednesday in a Thanksgiving holiday-shortened week.

Still, Friday’s market rout, driven by an unwinding of bets on artificial intelligence-led growth, prompted traders to pare expectations for a December hike as investors piled into Treasuries. Australian bonds tracked the moves early Monday, with yields falling about five basis points across the curve.

See also: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as Anthropic in focus

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Sunday that the Fed risks damaging the US economy by overtightening in response to the latest inflation data, pointing to signs of fragility in the financial system.

“Many people believe that they may be making a policy mistake if they overtighten,” Bessent told CBS’s Face The Nation, noting a series of hawkish comments from the central bank’s governors in recent weeks. “We’ve seen a substantial tightening in financial conditions over the past few months.”
